units.title: How programs get made
units.summary: What computers and programs are made of, how source code becomes an executable, the parts of a C++ program, the programming process, and how to plan with pseudocode, flowcharts and hierarchy charts.

lessons.title: Hardware and software
lessons.html:
One machine can handle a huge variety of tasks because it is programmable: it does whatever its program tells it to. A computer system has five major hardware parts: the CPU, main memory, secondary storage, input devices and output devices.

The CPU

The central processing unit runs program instructions. It has two parts: the control unit, which fetches each instruction and directs the other parts, and the arithmetic and logic unit (ALU), which does the math and comparisons. The CPU repeats the fetch/decode/execute cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode it to see what it asks for, execute it, then move to the next one. Today's CPUs are small chips called microprocessors.

Main memory

Main memory is random-access memory (RAM). A running program and the data it is using live here. RAM is divided into bytes; each byte is eight bits (bit is short for binary digit, a tiny switch that is on or off). Every byte has a unique number called its address; the CPU uses the address to find what it wants. (Later, a variable name in your program will stand for the address of the bytes that hold its value.) Addresses are consecutive numbers, like numbered post office boxes. RAM is volatile: when power goes off, its contents are lost.

Secondary storage

Disks, solid-state drives and flash drives hold programs and files for the long term. Secondary storage is nonvolatile, so it keeps data with the power off. It is bigger and cheaper per byte than RAM but much slower. That is why computers have both: RAM for fast working space, secondary storage for permanent copies. A program is copied from secondary storage into RAM before the CPU runs it.

Input and output devices

Input devices (keyboard, mouse, microphone, scanner) send data into the computer. Output devices (monitor, printer, speakers) send results out. A disk or USB drive counts as input when data is read from it and as output when data is saved to it.

Software

Software is the set of programs that tells the hardware what to do. There are two general categories:

  • System software controls and supports the computer itself: the operating system (the fundamental programs that manage hardware, memory and files and run other programs), utility programs (virus scanners, file compression, backup) and software development tools (compilers and editors).
  • Application software does work for the user: word processors, spreadsheets, email, browsers, games.

Exam trap: a browser or word processor is application software, not system software, even though the operating system runs it.

lessons.title: Programs, languages, compiling and linking
lessons.html:
A program is a list of instructions that the computer carries out to accomplish some job. An algorithm is a finite sequence of precisely stated steps that gets a job done or solves a problem. A program is an algorithm written in a language the computer can be made to run.

Machine language and programming languages

The only language a CPU runs directly is machine language: binary instructions specific to that CPU. Assembly language gives those instructions short names. Both are low-level: they match the hardware, and a program written for one CPU will not run on another. A high-level language such as C++ uses English-like statements and does not depend on one CPU. High-level programs are more portable: the same source code can be compiled for different systems, usually with few or no changes.

From source code to a running program

  1. You type source code into a source file (for C++, a .cpp file). You can use a text editor or an integrated development environment (IDE), which bundles a text editor, compiler, debugger and other tools under one set of menus (one click can preprocess, compile, link and run).
  2. The preprocessor reads the source file first and handles lines that begin with #, such as #include. These are preprocessor directives. The preprocessor pastes in the named file and produces the text the compiler will see.
  3. The compiler translates the program into machine language and writes an object file (object code). Syntax errors are found here, and no object file is produced if there are any.
  4. The linker merges the object file with the prewritten pieces the program needs from the runtime library, C++'s stock of ready-made code (for example the code behind cout), and produces the executable file. The compiler does not copy library code into the object file, so an object file holds only your own machine code and is not a complete program until it is linked. The runtime library is a large collection of prewritten code for common jobs such as screen output and math functions.
  5. The operating system loads the executable into RAM and the CPU runs it.

Order to memorize: source file, preprocessor, compiler, object file, linker, executable file. One command can run all three tools: g++ -o ship ship.cpp.

A compiler translates the whole program before it runs. That differs from an interpreter, which translates and runs one statement at a time.

#include <iostream>   // preprocessor directive
using namespace std;
int main()
{
    cout << "Hello" << endl;   // source code
    return 0;
}

lessons.title: What a C++ program is made of
lessons.html:
Every language has the same kinds of building blocks. Look at this program:

#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    double pounds, price, charge;   // variable definition
    cin >> pounds;
    cin >> price;
    charge = pounds * price;
    cout << "Charge: " << charge << endl;
    return 0;
}
ElementMeaningExamples above
Key words (reserved words)Words with a fixed meaning in C++. Always lowercase. Cannot be used for anything else.using, namespace, int, double, return
Programmer-defined identifiersNames you invent for variables and functions.pounds, price, charge
OperatorsSymbols that act on operands (usually data).=, *, <<, >>
PunctuationMarks the start or end of a statement or separates list items.; and , and { }
SyntaxThe rules for putting all of these together correctly.semicolon needed after a statement

main and cout are not key words. main is a special function name, and cout is an object from the iostream library. The = symbol is the assignment operator: it stores the value of the right side in the variable on the left.

Lines versus statements

A line is one row of text in the file. A statement is a full command telling the computer to take some action; in C++ most statements end with a semicolon. One statement may be spread over several lines, and one line may hold several statements. Blank lines and comments are lines but not statements. A comment starts with // (to end of line) or sits between /* and */; the compiler ignores it.

Variables

A variable is a location in memory that has been given a name. Its value can change while the program runs, and storing a new value replaces the old one. A variable definition states the type and name and creates the variable (double charge;). Define a variable before the first line that uses it. Numbers come in two general kinds: integers (whole numbers such as 5 or -129) and floating-point numbers (such as 6.7); double holds floating-point numbers.

Literals, operands and basic output

  • A literal is a value written directly in the code: 5, 12.5, or the string literal "Hello" in double quotes.
  • An operand is a value an operator acts on. In price * qty the operator is * and the operands are price and qty.
  • cout sends output to the screen. << is the stream insertion operator, and one cout statement can chain several items. cin >> reads input into a variable.
  • cout does not start a new line by itself. endl ends the current line, so the next output starts on a new line.
  • Several variables of one type can be defined in one statement, separated by commas, and a variable can be given a starting value in its definition: int apples = 3, pears = 4;.
  • Names are case-sensitive: Total and total are different identifiers. Key words are always lowercase.
int apples = 3, pears = 4;
cout << "Fruit: " << apples + pears << endl;   // Fruit: 7
cout << "No newline";
cout << "same line" << endl;                  // No newlinesame line

The assignment operator = is not the equality test; equality is written ==.

lessons.title: Input, processing, output, and the programming process
lessons.html:
Input, processing, output

Nearly every program does three things. Input is data the program receives from the outside world (keyboard, file, device); in C++ you use cin. Processing is what the program does to the data (calculations, comparisons). Output is what it sends out (screen, printer, file); in C++ you use cout. Defining a program means naming its purpose, input, processing and output.

The programming process

  1. State exactly what problem the program must solve.
  2. Visualize the program running (sketch the screens with sample input and output).
  3. Build a model with a hierarchy chart, flowchart or pseudocode.
  4. Check the model for logical errors.
  5. Type the code, save and compile it.
  6. Correct compile errors; repeat steps 5 and 6.
  7. Run the program with test data.
  8. Correct errors found while running; repeat steps 5 to 8.
  9. Validate the results: does the program really solve the original problem?

The emphasis is on planning: a good program starts with a design, not with typing. Desk-checking means stepping through the program by hand, writing down each variable's value and what is displayed after every statement. A logic error is a mistake that makes a program produce wrong results even though it compiles.

Procedural versus object-oriented

Procedural programming centers on procedures (in C++, functions): collections of statements that do one task, often sharing variables. Object-oriented programming (OOP) centers on objects. An object bundles data together with the procedures that work on that data, and you make an object do something by sending it a message (calling one of its functions). C++ supports both styles.

Software engineering covers the whole job: design, writing, testing, debugging, documenting and maintaining software. Top-down design splits a task into modules, which large projects hand to different teams.

Reading short programs in questions

Several definitions can share one statement, with starting values: double hours = 6, rate = 12.5, pay; gives hours 6, rate 12.5 and leaves pay without a defined value until it is assigned. When cout prints a double, it shows up to six significant digits and drops a useless decimal part, so a double holding 75 prints as 75, 2.5 prints as 2.5, and 1234567.0 prints as 1.23457e+06.

double d = 6 * 12.5;           // prints 75
cout << d << " " << 10.0 / 4;  // 75 2.5

Test data for the final steps is input you choose, with the correct answer worked out beforehand; validating the results means checking that the finished program solves the original problem stated in step 1.

lessons.title: Algorithms, pseudocode and hierarchy charts
lessons.book: Sections 1.3 and 1.6, pages 9 and 19 to 21; design tools
lessons.html:
An algorithm is a finite list of precise steps that solves a problem. Design tools let you work the algorithm out before writing C++.

Pseudocode

Pseudocode is a cross between English and a programming language. The computer cannot run it, there is no compiler for it and no official syntax, but good pseudocode is precise enough to translate line by line. Common conventions: Input or Read gets a value, Display or Print shows one, Set x = ... assigns, and If / Else / End If and While / End While mark selection and repetition, with indentation showing what is inside.

Input price
Input quantity
Set total = price * quantity
If total > 100
    Set total = total - 10
End If
Display total

Translating: Input becomes cin >>, Display becomes cout <<, Set becomes =, If becomes if (...) { }. Define the variables first.

double price, quantity, total;
cin >> price >> quantity;
total = price * quantity;
if (total > 100)
    total = total - 10;
cout << total << endl;

The three structures

  • Sequence: steps run one after another.
  • Selection: a condition picks which steps run (if, if/else).
  • Repetition (iteration): steps repeat while a condition holds (while, for).

Reading pseudocode

To find what pseudocode outputs, trace it: keep a column for each variable, update it line by line, and note each Display. Some questions state a program in plain English ("The variable x starts with 0. Add 1 to x. Display x."); trace those the same way. A common design error is a step placed too early, such as calculating a total before the values it uses have been input.

Hierarchy charts

A hierarchy chart shows the structure of a program: a box at the top for the overall task, with boxes below for the subtasks it divides into, and below those their subtasks. This is top-down design (divide and conquer). The chart shows what the parts are and how they nest, not the order of execution or any decisions. Subtasks often become functions or modules.

Details that questions rely on

  • Pseudocode arithmetic follows C++ precedence: multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, so a * a + b * b squares each first. Use parentheses to change the order.
  • A chain of choices is written If / Else If / Else / End If. The tests run top to bottom, only the first true test's steps run, and steps after End If run in every case.
  • Comparisons: >= means greater than or equal, != means not equal, and in C++ equality is ==. A single = assigns. if (age = 18) would store 18 instead of testing.
  • A While loop tests before each pass, and something inside the body must change the value the test uses, or the loop never ends. A loop that stops on a special entry reads once before the loop and again as the last step inside it.
  • Swapping two variables needs a third to hold one value temporarily; a = b; b = a; loses the old a.
  • Each step may only use values that already exist: put every Input step before the calculation that uses it. Prompts (Display) go before the Input they describe.
int num, sum = 0;
cin >> num;               // first read, before the loop
while (num != 0)
{
    sum = sum + num;
    cin >> num;           // next read, last step in the loop
}
cout << sum << endl;     // after the loop
int a = 5, b = 9, temp;
temp = a;  a = b;  b = temp;   // a is 9, b is 5

A flowchart's Start box is not part of a hierarchy chart; the top box of a hierarchy chart names the whole task, and the levels below name its subtasks.

lessons.title: Flowcharts
lessons.book: Section 1.6 and Appendix C material (written from standard practice)
lessons.html:
A flowchart is a diagram of the logical flow of a program. Each step is a shape and flow lines (arrows) join them to show the order.

ShapeNameUsed for
Oval (rounded rectangle)TerminalStart and End (or Stop)
ParallelogramInput/outputReading a value, displaying a value
RectangleProcessCalculations and assignments
DiamondDecisionA yes/no (true/false) question; two lines leave it, labeled Yes and No
Small circleConnectorContinues the chart elsewhere or on another page; matching labels join up (some standards draw a separate home-plate shape for an off-page connector)
Rectangle with an extra line inside each sidePredefined processA call to a module (function) charted separately

Flow lines normally run top to bottom, with arrowheads showing direction. A process, input or output box has one line in and one out; a decision has one in and two out. The chart has exactly one Start.

How the structures look

  • Sequence: boxes in a straight vertical line.
  • Selection: a diamond splits the flow into a Yes path and a No path. Both paths join again afterward. An if with no else has one empty path.
  • Repetition: a diamond tests a condition; the Yes path runs boxes and then a flow line loops back up to the diamond; the No path leaves the loop. A test at the top before the body is a pre-test loop, which is what C++ while is. If the boxes come first and the diamond comes after them, the body always runs at least once: a post-test loop, C++ do-while.

Example flowchart in words: Start; Input n; Set count = 1; Diamond "count <= n?"; Yes: Display count, Set count = count + 1, back to the diamond; No: End. In C++:

int n, count = 1;
cin >> n;
while (count <= n)
{
    cout << count << endl;
    count = count + 1;
}

Checking a flowchart means tracing it by hand, as in desk-checking. A loop whose flow line never leaves (the variable in the diamond never changes) is an infinite loop on paper too.

Traps when tracing

  • Integer division: when both operands are integers, / drops the fraction, so 5 / 2 is 2 and 20 / 6 is 3. % gives the remainder: 20 % 6 is 2. Halving 20 repeatedly gives 10, 5, 2, 1.
  • A post-test loop (body first, diamond after) always runs the body once, even when the test would have failed at the start. A pre-test loop may run zero times.
  • Two decisions drawn one after the other are both tested; they are not either/or unless the No path of the first leads around the second.
  • Translate by shape: parallelogram input is cin >>, parallelogram output is cout <<, a rectangle is an assignment or calculation, a diamond with two exits is if/else, and a diamond with a line returning to it is a loop.
int k = 5;
do
{
    cout << k << endl;    // runs once even though k < 5 is false
    k = k + 1;
} while (k < 5);

questions.prompt: Which hardware component fetches, decodes and executes program instructions?
choices: The CPU
Main memory
Secondary storage
The output device
questions.explain: The CPU runs the fetch/decode/execute cycle. Memory only holds instructions and data.

questions.prompt: What happens to the contents of main memory (RAM) when the computer is switched off?
choices: They are kept, because RAM is permanent storage
They are lost, because RAM is volatile
They are automatically moved to the CPU
They are sent to the output device
questions.explain: RAM needs power to hold data. Anything that must survive goes to secondary storage.

questions.prompt: The CPU has a control unit and a second unit that performs math and comparisons. Name it.
questions.explain: The ALU (arithmetic and logic unit) does calculations and comparisons; the control unit directs operations.

questions.prompt: Which of these is system software?
choices: A spreadsheet program
An email program
The operating system
A web browser
questions.explain: The operating system manages the computer itself. Spreadsheets, email programs and browsers do work for the user, so they are application software.

questions.prompt: Secondary storage such as a solid-state drive keeps its data when the power is off.
questions.explain: Secondary storage is nonvolatile. It is slower than RAM, so programs are copied into RAM to run.

questions.prompt: What does a compiler do?
choices: Combines object files with library code
Handles lines that begin with #
Runs the program one statement at a time
Translates source code into machine language (object code)
questions.explain: Compiling translates the whole source into object code. Combining with library code is the linker's job; # lines belong to the preprocessor.

questions.prompt: Which program combines your object file with library code to create the executable file?
choices: The linker
The preprocessor
The compiler
The editor
questions.explain: The linker joins the object file to the runtime library routines the program uses (such as the code behind cout) and writes the executable file. The compiler only makes the object file.

questions.prompt: Lines that begin with # (such as #include) are handled by the ___ before the compiler sees the code.
questions.explain: The preprocessor processes directives first and passes the resulting text to the compiler.

questions.prompt: Which pair of statements about languages is correct?
choices: C++ is low-level because it is compiled; machine language is portable
C++ is high-level and portable; machine language is low-level and specific to one kind of CPU
Both C++ and machine language are high-level but only C++ needs a compiler
C++ must be rewritten for each CPU; machine language runs on all CPUs
questions.explain: High-level languages hide hardware detail and compile for many CPUs. Machine language is binary instructions for one CPU family.

questions.prompt: Machine language is the only language a CPU can execute directly.
questions.explain: Everything else, including C++, must be translated to machine language first.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order for turning a C++ program into a running program?
choices: source file, compiler, preprocessor, linker, object file, executable file
source file, linker, object file, compiler, executable file
source file, preprocessor, compiler, object file, linker, executable file
source file, preprocessor, linker, compiler, executable file, object file
questions.explain: The preprocessor runs first, the compiler produces an object file, and the linker produces the executable. The compiler never makes the executable by itself.

questions.prompt: In the statement `int total = 5;` which item is a programmer-defined identifier?
questions.code: int total = 5;
choices: int
total
questions.explain: int is a key word, = is an operator, 5 is a literal. total is a name the programmer made up.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a C++ key word?
choices: cout
return
int
while
questions.explain: cout is an object defined in the iostream library, not a reserved word. return, int and while are reserved.

questions.prompt: In the statement `charge = pounds * price;` the = symbol is called the ___ operator.
questions.code: charge = pounds * price;
questions.explain: = stores the value on the right in the variable on the left. It is not the equality test, which is ==.

questions.prompt: How many statements are in this code?
questions.explain: A statement ends at its semicolon. The cout statement runs over two lines but is still one statement, plus the definition makes two.

questions.prompt: Every line of a C++ source file is exactly one statement.
questions.explain: Blank lines and comments are not statements, one statement can span several lines, and one line can hold several statements.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: The first two statements print AB and a newline. C then prints on the next line.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: The compiler ignores everything from // to end of line and everything between /* and */. Only the x and z statements run.

questions.prompt: The rules that say how key words, operators and punctuation may be combined in a language are called its ___.
questions.explain: Syntax errors are violations of these rules and the compiler reports them.

questions.prompt: A program asks the user for an age, works out the birth year, and shows the result on the screen. The step that takes the age from the keyboard is which of a program's three basic activities?
choices: Processing
Output
Input
Linking
questions.explain: Receiving data from the keyboard is input. Working out the birth year is processing and showing it is output; linking is a step in building the program, not something the running program does.

questions.prompt: According to the steps of the programming process, what comes first?
choices: Type the code and compile it
Run the program with test data
Check the results for validity
State exactly what problem the program must solve
questions.explain: Planning comes first: purpose, input, processing and output. Code is typed after the model is built and checked.

questions.prompt: A program reads a radius, calculates the area of a circle and displays it. Calculating the area is which activity?
choices: Processing
Input
Output
Compiling
questions.explain: Reading the radius is input, displaying is output, and the math in between is processing.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: hours times rate is 75. A double that holds a whole value prints without a decimal point by default.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes object-oriented programming compared with procedural programming?
choices: OOP is centered on functions that share data with each other
OOP is centered on objects that combine data with the functions that work on that data
OOP requires every program to have no variables
OOP means the program is designed with flowcharts only
questions.explain: Procedural programming centers on procedures. In OOP, each object carries its own data along with the procedures that work with it.

questions.prompt: What is desk-checking?
choices: Running the program on a very large input
Compiling the program on a second computer
Stepping through a program by hand, recording variable values and output after each statement
Asking the compiler to list all warnings
questions.explain: Desk-checking is a manual trace on paper. It finds logic errors before or after running the program.

questions.prompt: Is this legal? A program's first line inside `main` is `total = 5;`, and `int total;` appears two lines later. The compiler accepts it.
questions.explain: The compiler reads top to bottom, so the definition (type and name) must come before the first use. Here `total` is used before it exists, which is an error.

questions.prompt: A set of well-defined, ordered steps for solving a problem is called an ___.
questions.explain: An algorithm is the idea; a program is an algorithm written in a programming language.

questions.prompt: Pseudocode must follow strict syntax rules because the compiler checks it.
questions.explain: Pseudocode is for people. No compiler reads it and it has no official syntax, though it should be precise enough to translate.

questions.prompt: What does a hierarchy chart show?
choices: The exact order in which statements execute, with decisions
The values stored in each variable
The machine language produced by the compiler
The overall task broken down into subtasks, level by level
questions.explain: A hierarchy chart shows structure (top-down design). Execution order and decisions belong in flowcharts and pseudocode.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Set total = 0
Set i = 1
While i <= 5
    Set total = total + i
    Set i = i + 1
End While
Display total
questions.explain: The loop adds 1+2+3+4+5. When i becomes 6 the test fails and total, 15, is displayed.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Set a = 3
Set b = 8
Set temp = a
Set a = b
Set b = temp
Display a
Display b
questions.explain: temp saves 3, a takes 8, b takes the saved 3. The two values are swapped, and each Display is on its own line.

questions.prompt: Which C++ code matches this pseudocode?
questions.code:
Input age
If age >= 18
    Display "adult"
Else
    Display "minor"
End If
questions.explain: The pseudocode tests greater than or equal to 18 and has an Else. = assigns instead of comparing, > leaves out 18, and omitting else prints both words for adults.

questions.prompt: In a flowchart, the oval shape is used for the start and end points. What is it called?
questions.explain: The terminal symbol (an oval) marks where the flowchart begins and ends.

questions.prompt: In a flowchart, a parallelogram stands for a calculation (process).
questions.explain: A parallelogram is input or output. Calculations go in a rectangle.

questions.prompt: Which flowchart shape asks a yes/no question and has two exit lines?
choices: Rectangle
Diamond
Oval
Parallelogram
questions.explain: The decision diamond tests a condition and its two exits are labeled Yes and No (true and false).

questions.prompt: What is the small circle in a flowchart for?
choices: Start and end
Displaying output
A connector that continues the flow at another point or page
Making a calculation
questions.explain: Matching labeled circles join separate pieces of a flowchart. Start/end is an oval, output is a parallelogram.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Set n = 1; Diamond "n <= 3?"; Yes: Display n * n, Set n = n + 1, flow line back to the diamond; No: End. What does it display?
questions.code:
Start
Set n = 1
n <= 3 ?
  Yes: Display n * n
       Set n = n + 1
       (back to the test)
  No: End
questions.explain: The loop runs for n = 1, 2, 3 and shows 1, 4, 9. At n = 4 the No path ends the program.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Set x = 10; Diamond "x > 5?" Yes: Display "big"; No: skip. Both paths join. Diamond "x > 12?" Yes: Display "huge"; No: skip. Both paths join; End. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Start
Set x = 10
x > 5 ?   Yes: Display "big"
(paths join)
x > 12 ?  Yes: Display "huge"
(paths join)
End
questions.explain: Both decisions are tested one after the other. x > 5 is true so big shows; x > 12 is false so huge does not.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Input x (parallelogram); Diamond "x > 0?"; Yes: Display "positive"; No: Display "not positive"; End. Which C++ matches?
questions.explain: A diamond with two exit paths is if/else. Without else, not positive would always print too; a parallelogram labeled Input means cin; a loop would need a path back to the diamond.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Set n = 20; Set count = 0; Diamond "n > 1?"; Yes: Set n = n / 2 (integer division), Set count = count + 1, back to the diamond; No: Display count; End. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Start
Set n = 20
Set count = 0
n > 1 ?
  Yes: Set n = n / 2   (integer division)
       Set count = count + 1
       (back to the test)
  No: Display count
End
questions.explain: n goes 20, 10, 5, 2, 1 with the count at 4 when n reaches 1. Integer division makes 5 / 2 equal 2.

questions.prompt: This program is written as English statements. What would it display if it were a real program?
questions.code:
The variable p starts with the value 4.
The variable q starts with the value 7.
Add 3 to p.
Store the value of p times q in q.
Subtract p from q, and store the result in q.
Display the value in q.
questions.explain: p becomes 7, then q becomes 7 * 7 = 49, then 49 - 7 = 42. Each step uses the values left by the step before it.

questions.prompt: This program is written as English statements. What would it display if it were a real program?
questions.code:
Create three variables: a = 2, b = 9, c = 0.
Compute a plus b and put the answer in c.
Put c multiplied by 2 into a.
Put a plus c into b.
Show a, b and c on one line, separated by spaces.
questions.explain: c gets 2 + 9 = 11, then a gets 11 * 2 = 22 (the old 2 is gone), then b gets 22 + 11 = 33, replacing the 9.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode should ask for a ticket price and a quantity, then display the total cost. What is the error?
questions.code:
Set cost = price * quantity
Display "Enter the ticket price"
Input price
Display "Enter the quantity"
Input quantity
Display cost
choices: Every Display must come after all of the Input steps
The multiplication should be an addition
cost is calculated before price and quantity have been input
Pseudocode lines must end with semicolons
questions.explain: A step can only use values that already exist. The Set cost line belongs after both Input steps; as written it multiplies values that have not been entered yet. Prompts (Display) before each Input are correct.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Display "Card value? " (parallelogram); Input value (parallelogram); Display "Amount spent? " (parallelogram); Input spent (parallelogram); Set remain = value - spent (rectangle); Display remain (parallelogram); End. Which C++ matches?
questions.explain: The steps run top to bottom: each Input parallelogram becomes cin, and the process rectangle subtracts spent from value after both are read. Calculating first would use values not yet entered, and cout cannot read input.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Set temp = 68
If temp > 80
    Display "hot"
Else If temp > 60
    Display "mild"
Else
    Display "cold"
End If
Display "done"
questions.explain: 68 > 80 is false, so the next test runs: 68 > 60 is true and mild is shown. The chain stops at the first true test, and done is shown after End If either way.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Set n = 10
While n > 0
    Display n
    Set n = n - 3
End While
questions.explain: n is shown, then reduced by 3: 10, 7, 4, 1. After 1 it becomes -2, the test n > 0 fails, and the loop ends without showing -2.

questions.prompt: A flowchart reads: Start; Set k = 5; Display k; Set k = k + 1; Diamond "k < 5?"; Yes: flow line back up to Display k; No: End. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Start
Set k = 5
Display k        <-----+
Set k = k + 1          |
k < 5 ?   Yes ---------+
  No: End
questions.explain: The diamond comes after the body, so this is a post-test loop (a do-while in C++): the body runs once before the first test. k becomes 6, 6 < 5 is false, and the chart ends.

questions.prompt: Which C++ code matches this pseudocode?
questions.code:
Set sum = 0
Input num
While num != 0
    Set sum = sum + num
    Input num
End While
Display sum
questions.explain: Both Input steps are needed: one before the loop and one as the last step inside it, and Display sum comes after End While. Dropping the inner input makes an infinite loop, if runs the steps at most once, and output inside the loop shows a running total.

questions.prompt: This pseudocode is run and the user types 3 and then 4. What is displayed?
questions.code:
Input a
Input b
Set c = a * a + b * b
Display c
questions.explain: a is 3 and b is 4, so c is 9 + 16 = 25. Multiplication is done before addition, just as in C++.

questions.prompt: In a flowchart, a diamond's Yes path runs some boxes and then a flow line goes back up to the same diamond. Which structure is this?
choices: Sequence
Selection
A connector
Repetition (a loop)
questions.explain: A flow line that returns to an earlier decision makes steps repeat, so it is a loop. Selection also uses a diamond, but its two paths join below it and never go back up.

questions.prompt: You are drawing the flowchart for a program that reads a price and a tax rate, calculates the tax, and displays it. Which shape holds the step `tax = price * rate`?
choices: Parallelogram
Rectangle
Diamond
Oval
questions.explain: Calculations and assignments are processes, drawn as rectangles. Reading the price and rate and displaying the tax go in parallelograms.

questions.prompt: A program reads a starting balance, the total of deposits, the total of withdrawals and a monthly interest rate, then calculates and displays the current balance. In its hierarchy chart, which box belongs at the very top?
choices: Read the total of deposits
Display the balance
Start
Find the current account balance
questions.explain: The top box names the whole task. Getting the input, calculating and displaying are subtasks on the level below it. Start is a flowchart terminal, not part of a hierarchy chart.

questions.prompt: In standard flowcharting, what does a rectangle with an extra vertical line just inside each side stand for?
choices: A predefined process: a call to a module or function that is charted separately
An input step
Two calculations done at the same time
The end of the program
questions.explain: The predefined process symbol shows a call to a module (function) whose steps are charted elsewhere. A plain rectangle is an ordinary process; input is a parallelogram and the end is an oval.

questions.prompt: One computer can run a game, a spreadsheet and a browser because its behavior is set by whatever instructions it is given: it is ___ (one word).
questions.explain: A computer is not built for one job. It does whatever job its program tells it to do.

questions.prompt: Which statement about main memory is correct?
choices: Each byte has a unique address, and each byte is made of eight bits
Bytes have no addresses; the CPU searches memory for the data it needs
Each bit has its own address, and a byte is two bits
A byte is sixteen bits, and only the first byte has an address
questions.explain: Memory is divided into bytes of 8 bits (bit is short for binary digit). Every byte has its own number, its address, which the CPU uses to find it.

questions.prompt: Each byte of main memory is identified by a unique number called its ___.
questions.explain: Addresses run from lowest to highest, like numbered post office boxes. A variable's name stands for the address where its value is stored.

questions.prompt: A virus scanner, a file-compression program and a backup program are all examples of which kind of software?
choices: Application software
Operating systems
Software development tools
Utility programs, a kind of system software
questions.explain: Utility programs do a specialized job that improves the computer's operation or protects data. The textbook classes them as system software, not application software.

questions.prompt: Source code written in a high-level language can usually be recompiled for a different kind of CPU with little or no editing. That property is called being ___.
questions.explain: C++ is portable: the same source code can be recompiled for another system with little or no change. Machine language is not portable.

questions.prompt: An object file can be run by itself, because the compiler has already translated it into machine language.
questions.explain: The object file holds machine code but not the runtime library routines the program uses (such as the code behind cout). The linker must add them to make the executable file.

questions.prompt: Words such as int, double and return have a special meaning in C++ and may be used only for that purpose. They are called key words or ___ words.
questions.explain: Key words are reserved for the language and are always lowercase. You cannot use one as a variable name.

questions.prompt: In the statement `total = price * qty;` which symbols are operators?
choices: ; and =
only *
= and *
* and ;
questions.explain: = (assignment) and * (multiplication) act on operands. The semicolon is punctuation: it marks the end of the statement.

questions.prompt: A named storage location in memory, whose value can change while the program runs, is a ___.
questions.explain: The name stands for a location in RAM. Storing a new value replaces the old one.

questions.prompt: In the nine-step programming process, which step comes right before typing the code?
choices: Run the program with test data
Check the model for logical errors
Validate the results
Correct errors found while running
questions.explain: The order is: define, visualize, model with design tools, check the model for logic errors, and only then type, save and compile. Testing and validating come after the code compiles.

questions.prompt: When you clearly define what a program is to do, which four items do you identify?
choices: Purpose, input, processing and output
Sequence, selection, repetition and hierarchy
Source code, object code, library and executable
Variables, constants, functions and objects
questions.explain: Step 1 names what the program is for, what goes in, what is done to it, and what comes out.

questions.prompt: Visualizing a program running means picturing, or sketching, its screens with sample input and output before you write the code.
questions.explain: Putting yourself in the user's place this way decides what the program will ask and display, which settles most of its output early.

questions.prompt: What is an integrated development environment (IDE)?
choices: A collection of prewritten library code that the linker adds
The part of the operating system that loads programs into memory
A program that translates and runs one statement at a time
One package that combines a text editor, compiler, debugger and other tools under a single set of menus
questions.explain: In an IDE one click can preprocess, compile, link and run. Prewritten code is the runtime library, and translating one statement at a time describes an interpreter.

questions.prompt: The large collection of prewritten C++ code for jobs like screen output and math functions, which the linker joins to your object code, is called the ___ library.
questions.explain: The compiler does not put library code into the object file; the linker adds the library routines the program uses.

questions.prompt: Which part of the CPU coordinates the computer's operations and determines where to get the next instruction?
choices: The arithmetic and logic unit
Main memory
The control unit
Secondary storage
questions.explain: The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals to the other parts. The ALU only does the math and comparisons.

questions.prompt: In what order does the CPU handle each instruction of a program?
choices: Fetch, decode, execute
Execute, decode, fetch
Fetch, execute, decode
Decode, fetch, execute
questions.explain: The control unit fetches the next instruction from main memory, decodes it to see what it asks for, and then the right component executes it. The cycle repeats for every instruction.

units.title: Testing and debugging
units.summary: Kinds of errors, hand tracing, choosing test data, the classic C++ bug patterns, and stubs and drivers.

lessons.title: Kinds of errors and what the compiler tells you
lessons.book: Sections 1.6 and 3.10, pages 21 and 133; general debugging
lessons.html:
Debugging is finding and fixing the errors in a program. Errors fall into three main families, plus linker errors.

KindWhen it shows upExample
Syntax errorAt compile time. The compiler reports it with a line number and no executable is made.missing semicolon, misspelled key word, undefined variable, unmatched brace
Logic errorThe program compiles and runs but gives wrong results.wrong formula, = instead of ==, loop that runs one time too few
Linker errorAfter compiling, when the object file is linked. No executable is made.a function that has a prototype and is called but was never defined
Run-time errorWhile the program runs: it crashes or stops abnormally.integer division by zero (undefined behavior; on most systems it stops the program), running out of memory

Many textbooks, including Gaddis, use "runtime error" loosely for any mistake found while running, which includes wrong answers. On an exam, decide by the symptom: it will not compile is a syntax error; it runs but the answer is wrong is a logic error; it crashes is a run-time error.

Errors versus warnings

An error stops compilation. A warning does not: the compiler still builds the program, but it is telling you the code is legal and probably wrong. Typical warnings: a variable that is never used, a variable that may be used before it is set, a comparison between signed and unsigned values, and an assignment inside an if condition. Treat every warning as a possible logic error and fix it. Turning on more warnings (for g++, -Wall) catches bugs early.

What the compiler cannot find

The compiler checks the rules of the language, not your intent. A program with no errors and no warnings can still print the wrong thing. Only testing, hand tracing and careful reading find logic errors.

C++ is case-sensitive: Cout or Return is a compile error, not a typo the compiler forgives. A single missing brace or semicolon often causes a flood of messages that begin on the line after the real mistake, so fix the first error, then recompile.

int total = 0           // syntax error: missing ;
cout << total / 0;     // would be a run-time error for int
average = a + b / 2;    // logic error if you meant (a + b) / 2

More on warnings and messages

  • By default a warning does not stop the build. With the g++ option -Werror every warning is treated as an error.
  • A message such as "undefined reference to computeTotal" comes from the linker: the call was accepted by the compiler because a prototype exists, but no function body was ever supplied.
  • Syntax errors include: an undefined (never declared) name, a misspelled key word, a wrong capital letter, an unmatched brace or parenthesis, and a missing semicolon.
  • "Runtime error" is the usual textbook name for any mistake that shows only while the finished program executes. Strictly, a wrong answer is a logic error, and a crash is a run-time error.

lessons.title: Hand tracing and desk-checking
lessons.html:
Hand tracing is a debugging technique where you pretend to be the computer and execute the program one statement at a time on paper. Chapter 1 calls the same process desk-checking: stepping through the code on paper, writing down each variable's contents and what is displayed after each statement. It is especially good at finding math mistakes and other logic errors.

How to do it

  1. Set up a table in which every variable gets its own column and every statement you execute gets its own row.
  2. Pick sample input whose correct answer you can work out in advance.
  3. Go statement by statement. After each one, write the new value in that variable's column. A value stays until some statement changes it.
  4. Write down what is displayed after every output statement.
  5. Compare the result with the answer you expected. The first row where the chart goes wrong points to the bug.

Example of a bug found by tracing:

double n1, n2, n3, avg;
n1 = 10; n2 = 20; n3 = 30;
avg = n1 + n2 + n3 / 3;
after statementn1n2n3avg
n1 = 1010???
n2 = 201020??
n3 = 30102030?
avg = ...10203040

A correct average would be 20, but the chart shows 40. Division has higher precedence than addition, so only n3 was divided: 10 + 20 + 10 = 40. The fix is (n1 + n2 + n3) / 3.

Tracing loops

For a loop, add a row for each pass and include the loop variable. Record the value the condition sees each time it is tested, including the final test that fails. Count passes carefully: a loop from 1 while i <= 4 runs 4 times; while i < 4 it runs 3.

Tracing also verifies a flowchart or pseudocode before any code is written, which is step 4 of the programming process.

Operators you will trace

  • / on two int values drops the fraction. % is the remainder (10 % 3 is 1), so n % 2 == 0 tests for an even number.
  • x++ adds 1 to x. x += i means x = x + i. != means not equal.
  • for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) sets i to 1 once, tests i <= 4 before every pass, and adds 1 to i after every pass; the loop ends when the test is false.
  • For input in a loop, cin >> num takes the next value typed; a loop that ends on an entry such as 0 does not process that final 0.
int n = 10, steps = 0;
while (n != 1)
{
    if (n % 2 == 0) n = n / 2;
    else            n = 3 * n + 1;
    steps++;
}
// n is 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: the body ran 6 times

To swap, a hand trace of a = b; b = a; with a = 5 and b = 9 shows both ending as 9: after the first statement the old 5 no longer exists anywhere.

lessons.title: Choosing test data
lessons.book: Section 1.6 (pages 21 and 22) and 3.10, plus general testing practice
lessons.html:
Testing means running a program with sample input to see whether the output is right. Passing one test proves little. A good set of test cases each has an input and the expected output that you worked out by hand before running. If you take the program's own output as correct, you will never notice that it is wrong.

Three kinds of test data

  • Normal (typical) data: ordinary values well inside the allowed range, such as 72 for a score that may be 0 to 100.
  • Boundary data: values at, just inside, and just outside the edges of a range, where off-by-one mistakes (< versus <=) hide. For a valid range of 0 to 100: 0, 1, 99, 100, and the outside neighbors -1 and 101. For a rule like "60 or more passes": 59, 60, 61.
  • Invalid data: input the program should reject or handle, such as a negative age, letters where a number is expected, or zero when it will be a divisor.

Also test the special cases for the problem: an empty list, a count of 0 or 1, all values equal, the largest and smallest values.

Coverage

Every path in the program should run at least once. If there is an if, test one input that makes it true and one that makes it false. If there is a loop, test it running zero times (if possible), once, and many times. For an if/else-if chain with four branches, you need at least four inputs, one per branch, plus the boundaries between branches.

Example

// Pass if score is 60 or more
if (score > 60)          // bug: should be >=
    cout << "pass";
else
    cout << "fail";

Test scores 40 and 90 both give correct answers. Only the boundary test, 60, shows that this prints "fail" when it should say "pass".

Testing can show that bugs exist; it can never prove that none remain. Finally, validate the results: check that the program solves the original problem, not just that it matches your design.

Putting a test set together

"Random data" is not one of the three standard kinds; the kinds are normal, boundary and invalid. A branch chain such as child (under 13), teen (13 to 19) and adult (20 or more) has its boundaries on both sides of each cut-off: 12 and 13, then 19 and 20. Typical values (5, 15, 40) run each branch once but would not expose a < written where <= belongs. A loop that totals n numbers should be tried with n = 0, n = 1, and a typical larger n.

lessons.title: Common bug patterns in C++
lessons.book: General debugging practice (no single book section); relates to Chapters 4 and 5
lessons.html:
These mistakes appear again and again, and exams love them. Most of them compile.

1. = versus ==

if (x = 5) assigns 5 to x and the condition is the value 5, which is true. It is always true (for any nonzero value) and it changes x. Use == to compare.

2. Stray semicolon

if (x > 10); ends the if with an empty statement. The next statement then runs every time. while (i < 3); makes an empty body, so a loop that should end now loops forever. for (...); repeats nothing and then runs the block once.

3. Missing braces

Without { }, an if, else or loop controls only the one statement after it. Indentation does not matter to the compiler. The second line below always runs.

if (n > 0)
    cout << "positive ";
    cout << "done";      // always runs

4. Missing break

In a switch, execution falls through into the next case until a break (or the end). Forgetting it prints extra output.

5. Integer division

When both operands are int, / drops the fraction: 7 / 2 is 3, and double r = 7 / 2; stores 3.0. Make at least one operand a double: 7 / 2.0 or static_cast<double>(7) / 2. Also % works only on integers.

6. Uninitialized variable or accumulator

A local variable has no defined starting value. int sum; sum += x; adds to garbage. Start totals at 0 and products at 1.

7. Off-by-one

for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) runs n + 1 times; for (i = 1; i < n; i++) runs n - 1 times. Decide which and check the boundaries.

8. Operator precedence

a + b / 2 divides only b. Add parentheses when you mean something else. Note also && binds tighter than ||. A range test written x < 0 && x > 100 can never be true; "outside the range" needs ||.

9. Others

Comparing doubles with == (they hold approximations, so compare the difference to a small tolerance), a while loop whose body never changes the variable it tests (an infinite loop), forgetting to read input before using it, and using the wrong variable (a copy-paste slip) are common too.

Syntax these examples use

  • switch (choice) jumps to the matching case label and keeps running statements downward until a break or the closing brace. default: runs when no case matches (and, if there is no break above it, also by falling through).
  • x++ adds 1; sum += i means sum = sum + i. for (init; test; update) runs init once, tests before every pass, and runs update after every pass.
  • && means AND (both sides true) and || means OR (at least one side true).
  • fabs (from <cmath>) gives the absolute value of a double, used for tolerance tests such as fabs(total - 0.3) < 0.0001.
  • When cout prints a double it drops a pointless decimal part: 3.0 prints as 3, 3.5 as 3.5.
  • The condition of an if or loop is true for any nonzero value and false for 0, so if (x = 0) is false and if (x = 5) is true. g++ with -Wall warns about an assignment used as a condition.
  • A for loop with a stray semicolon, for (...);, has an empty body; the indented statement after it runs once, after the loop. Two statements at the same indentation after a brace-less for or if are not both controlled by it.
int x = 7, total = 0;
x++;                              // x is 8
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
    total += i;                   // total is 6
double r = 7 / 2, s = 7 / 2.0;    // 3 and 3.5
switch (2)
{
    case 1: cout << "one";  break;
    case 2: cout << "two";  break;
    default: cout << "other";
}

An off-by-one error is a loop that runs one time too many or too few, usually from < versus <= or the wrong starting value.

lessons.title: Stubs and drivers
lessons.book: Section 6.16, pages 372 and 373; debugger use from general practice
lessons.html:
When a program is split into functions, you can test the pieces in isolation. Two small tools help.

Stub

A stub is a dummy function used in place of a real function that is not written (or not trusted) yet. It usually does nothing except display a message that it was called, often with the argument values it received. If the real function returns a value, the stub returns a fixed test value so the calling code can continue. Stubs let you test the calling code: is the function called when expected, and are the right values passed?

double getTax(double amount)      // stub
{
    cout << "getTax called with " << amount << endl;
    return 10.0;                  // fixed test value
}

Driver

A driver is a small program (or a main function) whose only job is to call one function with test data and show what comes back. Drivers test the function itself, apart from the rest of the program.

int main()                        // driver for square()
{
    cout << square(3) << endl;     // expect 9
    cout << square(-2) << endl;    // expect 4
    cout << square(0) << endl;     // expect 0
    return 0;
}

Which when

ToolReplacesTests
Stubthe functionthe code that calls it
Driverthe caller (main)the function

Build incrementally: write and test one function at a time. Stubs let you run a whole program early; drivers let you check each real function with chosen normal, boundary and invalid inputs. When the pieces work, replace the stubs with the real functions and run the full program.

Other debugging aids

A temporary cout that prints variable values at key points (for a loop, on every pass) shows where a program first goes wrong. Remove or comment out these diagnostic lines when done.

A debugger (built into most IDEs) does the hand trace for you: set a breakpoint on a line and the program pauses there; step runs one statement at a time; a watch shows chosen variables' current values while the program is paused.

Reading the examples

  • A function is defined above main (or declared there with a prototype) so main can call it. return sends a value back to the caller, which can use the call as a value: price + getTax(price).
  • An array holds several values of one type; int tests[3] = {3, -2, 0}; makes three elements numbered 0, 1 and 2, and tests[i] is one element. A driver often loops over an array of test values.
  • A stub's message appears each time the stub is called, in the order the calls happen, mixed with the caller's own output.
  • A driver tests a function you have written; if the function does not exist yet, use a stub for it. A stub that stands in for an int function must still return an int, normally a fixed test value.
  • Statements you add only to see values (diagnostic cout lines) should print the pass number, the value just read and the running total inside the loop, so the first wrong value shows which pass failed. Remove them when the bug is fixed.
int total(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int main()
{
    int tests[3] = {3, -2, 0};
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        cout << tests[i] << " " << total(tests[i], 1) << endl;   // driver
    return 0;
}

questions.prompt: A program has a missing semicolon at the end of a statement. What kind of error is this?
choices: Logic error
Syntax error
Run-time error
Validation error
questions.explain: The compiler rejects code that breaks the language rules, so it never produces an executable. Logic and run-time errors need a program that compiles.

questions.prompt: A program compiles with no messages and runs to the end, but it prints 7 where the correct answer is 5. What kind of error is it?
choices: Syntax error
Compiler warning
Logic error
Linker error
questions.explain: Nothing stopped it from running; it just computes the wrong thing. Only testing or tracing can find it.

questions.prompt: A program compiles, but when run it crashes at the moment it divides an int by an int variable that holds 0. What kind of error is this?
questions.code:
int a = 10, b = 0;
cout << a / b;
choices: Syntax error
Logic error caught by the compiler
Preprocessor error
Run-time error
questions.explain: The mistake appears only while running and stops the program abnormally. The compiler cannot know the variable will be 0. (Integer division by zero is undefined behavior in C++; on most systems it ends the program.)

questions.prompt: A compiler warning, unlike a compiler error, does not by itself stop the executable file from being created.
questions.explain: Warnings are not errors, so the build finishes (unless you tell the compiler to treat warnings as errors, for example g++ -Werror). They often point at real logic bugs, so read them.

questions.prompt: A mistake that lets a program compile and run but produces wrong results is called a ___ error.
questions.explain: The compiler checks the grammar, not the intent. Wrong formulas and wrong conditions are logic errors.

questions.prompt: Hand trace this code. What does it print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: n3 / 3 is evaluated first and is 6, so avg is 6 + 12 + 6 = 24. The intended average, 12, needs parentheses around the sum.

questions.prompt: Hand trace this code. What does it print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
The programmer meant to swap a and b. What does this print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: After a = b, a is 9 and the old 5 is gone. Then b = a copies 9 again. Swapping needs a temporary variable.

questions.prompt: Stepping through a program by hand and writing down each variable's value after each statement is called hand tracing or ___-checking.
questions.explain: Desk-checking uses a chart with a column per variable. It finds logic errors without running the program.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body of this loop run?
questions.explain: n goes 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: the body runs for each change, six times, and the loop stops when n reaches 1.

questions.prompt: Which kind of test data is a value at the very edge of the allowed range, such as 0 or 100 when scores must be 0 to 100?
choices: Normal data
Boundary data
Invalid data
Random data
questions.explain: Boundary values catch < versus <= mistakes. Values outside the range, such as -1 or 101, are invalid data.

questions.prompt: A function accepts a percentage from 0 to 100 inclusive. Which set of test inputs is best?
questions.explain: A good set includes normal data, both boundaries, their neighbors, and invalid values on both sides.

questions.prompt: Input the program should reject, such as an age of -5, is called ___ test data.
questions.explain: Invalid data checks that the program handles bad input instead of failing or accepting it.

questions.prompt: If a program gives the right output for one test run, that proves the program is correct.
questions.explain: Testing can show that bugs exist but never that none remain. Test normal, boundary and invalid cases and every branch.

questions.prompt: The program should pass anyone with 60 or more. What does it print for the boundary value 60? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: 60 is not greater than 60, so the else branch runs. The bug is > where >= was needed, and only a boundary test exposes it.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: x = 5 assigns 5, and the value of the expression is 5, which is true. So the message prints and x is now 5.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: The semicolon ends the if with an empty statement. The cout is a separate statement that always runs.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: Without braces only the first cout belongs to the if. The second always runs regardless of the indentation.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: Case 2 matches and with no break execution falls through into case 3, which does have a break.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: a / b is integer division giving 3 before it is stored in the double. Casting one operand first makes the division floating-point.

questions.prompt: What is the bug in this code?
choices: The loop runs one time too many
The variable i should be a double
sum should be declared after the loop
sum starts with an unpredictable value because it was never initialized
questions.explain: A local int has no defined starting value, so the accumulator needs sum = 0. The loop bounds here are fine.

questions.prompt: The code is meant to add 1 through 5. What does it print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: With i < 5 the loop stops before 5, adding 1+2+3+4 = 10. The fix is i <= 5.

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: The loop never ends and nothing is printed, because the semicolon is the loop body
It prints 0 1 2
It prints 0 1 2 3
It prints nothing and ends normally
questions.explain: while (i < 3); is a loop with an empty body; i never changes, so the condition stays true forever. The braced block after it is not part of the loop.

questions.prompt: A dummy function that stands in for a real one and usually just displays a message that it was called is a ___.
questions.explain: Stubs let you test the code that calls a function before the function is written.

questions.prompt: A small program that tests a function by calling it with test data and displaying the result is a ___.
questions.explain: A driver lets you try the function out by itself, apart from everything else the program does.

questions.prompt: A stub usually displays a message showing that it was called, rather than doing the real work.
questions.explain: A stub only needs to show that it was reached and with what arguments, plus return a test value if the real function returns one.

questions.prompt: You wrote main() with a menu but have not written the calcFee function yet. What should you use to test the menu logic?
choices: A driver for calcFee
A stub for calcFee
A second compiler
A larger set of boundary data for the menu only
questions.explain: A stub replaces the missing function so main can run and you can see it is called with the right arguments. A driver would test calcFee, which does not exist yet.

questions.prompt: This program uses a stub for getTax. What does it print?
questions.explain: The stub displays its message and returns the fixed test value 10, so the total is 200 + 10.

questions.prompt: This main() is a driver for the function square. What does it print?
questions.explain: A driver just calls the function with chosen test values and shows the results.

questions.prompt: A stub for a function that returns an int should normally:
choices: Return nothing, so the caller notices the failure
Contain the full finished algorithm
Display a message and return a fixed test value
Call main() to test itself
questions.explain: The caller needs some value to continue; a fixed test value lets you check how the caller uses the result.

questions.prompt: A program contains the prototype `double computeTotal(double);` and calls computeTotal, but the function body was never written. Compiling the .cpp file succeeds, yet building the executable fails with "undefined reference to computeTotal". Which step reported the error?
choices: The preprocessor
The linker
The running program
The compiler's syntax check
questions.explain: The prototype satisfies the compiler, so an object file is made. When the linker tries to connect the call to the function's code, it finds none and stops, so no executable is produced.

questions.prompt: The compiler lists 14 errors. The first one is on line 9, where a statement is missing its semicolon. What is the best next step?
choices: Fix the missing semicolon, then recompile and see which errors remain
Fix all 14 errors, starting with the last one listed
Run the program anyway, since only one line is really wrong
Delete line 9 and every other line the messages mention
questions.explain: One missing semicolon or brace confuses the compiler about the lines that follow and produces a cascade of messages. Fixing the first error often makes many of the others disappear.

questions.prompt: A student types `Cout << "Total";` with a capital C. What happens?
choices: It runs normally, because C++ ignores capitalization
It compiles, but prints nothing at run time
It compiles and runs, but the output is wrong (a logic error)
The compiler reports an error, because C++ is case-sensitive and Cout is not defined
questions.explain: C++ treats Cout and cout as different names. Cout was never declared, so this is a compile-time (syntax) error and no executable is made.

questions.prompt: A syntax error is reported by the compiler. A mistake that shows itself only once the finished program is executing is called a runtime error.
questions.explain: It shows up only when the program is executed, unlike a syntax error, which the compiler finds. Gaddis notes runtime errors are usually logic errors such as a math mistake; a crash such as integer division by zero also appears only at run time.

questions.prompt: The code should print "out of range" for any score below 0 or above 100. What does it print when score is 150? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: No number is both below 0 and above 100, so the && condition is always false and the else runs. The test needs ||: score < 0 || score > 100.

questions.prompt: After `double total = 0.1 + 0.2;` a program tests `if (total == 0.3)`. Why is this test a bug risk?
choices: == cannot be used with double values, so it is a compile error
0.1 + 0.2 is computed as an integer, giving 0
Doubles store most decimal fractions approximately, so the sum may differ from 0.3 in its last bits and the test can be false
An if statement needs braces when it compares doubles
questions.explain: Values like 0.1 have no exact binary form, so tiny rounding differences appear. Compare doubles by checking that the difference is within a small tolerance, such as fabs(total - 0.3) < 0.0001.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this loop?
choices: It prints 1 2 3 4 5 and stops
i is never changed inside the loop, so the condition stays true and it prints 1 forever
It never runs, because i starts at 1
It runs 4 times, because of <=
questions.explain: A loop must change something its condition tests. Adding i++; inside the braces makes it print 1 to 5 and stop.

questions.prompt: In a debugger, what is a breakpoint?
choices: A line marked so the program pauses there, letting you examine variables before continuing
A line where the compiler found a syntax error
The point where the program crashes
A comment that tells the compiler to skip a line
questions.explain: When execution reaches a breakpoint it stops. You can then look at (watch) variables and step through the following statements one at a time.

questions.prompt: A debugger can show you the variables' values only after the program has finished running.
questions.explain: A debugger pauses the running program, at a breakpoint or one statement at a time (stepping), and shows current values while it is paused. It is an automated hand trace.

questions.prompt: A loop that totals 10 input values gives the wrong total. Which temporary debugging statement gives the most useful information?
choices: A cout inside the loop that prints the pass number, the value just read and the running total on each pass
A cout before the loop that prints "starting"
A cout after the loop that prints the final total
A cout at the end of main that prints "done"
questions.explain: Printing the values on every pass shows the exact pass where the total first goes wrong. Remove or comment out such diagnostic lines once the bug is fixed.

questions.prompt: Hand trace this code. The user types 4 9 2 7 0. What does it print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: The loop handles 4, 9, 2 and 7, then reads 0 and stops, so count is 4. best changes to 4 and then to 9; 2 and 7 are not larger.

questions.prompt: A program prints child for ages below 13, teen for 13 to 19, and adult for 20 and over. Which set of test ages checks the boundaries between the branches?
questions.explain: Boundary tests sit on both sides of each cut-off: 12 and 13, then 19 and 20. 5, 15 and 40 run each branch once but would miss a < written where <= was needed.

questions.prompt: A loop reads n numbers and totals them. Which values of n best test the loop?
choices: Only a typical value such as 8
Several typical values such as 7, 8 and 9
0, 1 and a typical larger value such as 8
Only the largest value the program allows
questions.explain: Test a loop running zero times, once, and many times. The 0 and 1 cases catch a wrong starting value or an off-by-one test that typical values hide.

questions.prompt: It is fine to run the program first and then use its output as the expected result for each test case.
questions.explain: Expected output must be worked out by hand before running. Otherwise a wrong answer simply becomes the expected one and the test can never fail.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: x = 0 stores 0 in x, and the condition takes that value, 0, which is false, so the else runs. x is now 0. g++ -Wall warns about an assignment used as a condition, a hint that == was meant.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: Without braces only the first cout is the loop body. The indented cout << "x" is a separate statement that runs once, after the loop ends.

questions.prompt: A loop that runs one time too many or one time too few has an ___ error.
questions.explain: It usually comes from the wrong comparison (< versus <=) or the wrong starting value. Boundary tests catch it.
