lessons.title: Procedural versus object-oriented programming
lessons.book: Sections 1.7 and 13.1, pages 22 to 23 and 751 to 757
lessons.html:
In procedural programming the program is built around procedures (functions in C++). The data sits in separate variables and structures that are passed to the functions. The data and the code that works on it are separate things. When the data format changes, every function that touches it may have to change, which breeds bugs in large programs.

In object-oriented programming (OOP) the program is built around objects. An object is a unit of software that packages some data together with the procedures that act on that data.

  • The data in an object are its attributes (C++ calls them member variables).
  • The procedures it performs are its member functions. Other languages call them methods.

Encapsulation and data hiding

Encapsulation means bundling the data with the code that works on it inside one object. Data hiding means an object can hide its data from code outside the object. Only the object's own member functions access the data directly; outside code uses the member functions as a simple interface. A car works like this: you use the pedals and wheel, not the linkages under the hood. Hidden data is protected from accidental corruption, and the inside of an object can be redesigned without breaking the code that uses it.

Class versus object

A class is code that describes the attributes and member functions a type of object has. It is a blueprint. It uses no memory for data by itself. An object is built from the class and holds real values. Each such object is an instance of its class. You can make many instances of one class, and each has its own copy of the attributes. Many houses can be built from one blueprint.

Reusability

An object is not a program by itself; it is used by programs. Because an object hides its inner workings behind an interface, the same class can be reused in many programs. Your code already uses objects written by others: cin and cout.

C++ supports both styles. In this unit you only need classes with data and member functions. No inheritance, pointers or operator overloading.

Using a class someone else wrote

string is a class, and a string variable is an object of it. You call a member function through the object with the dot operator: word.length() returns the number of characters and word.append("house") adds text to the end of the stored string. You never see how the text is stored, which is data hiding and reuse at work.

string word = "tree";
word.append("house");
cout << word << " " << word.length();   // treehouse 9

Terms to know

TermMeaning
Procedural programmingbuilt around procedures (functions); data and code are separate
Object-oriented programmingbuilt around objects that combine data and procedures
Attribute / member variablea piece of data in an object
Member function (method)a procedure that belongs to an object's class
Encapsulationcombining data and the code that works on it in one object
Data hidingkeeping data out of direct reach of outside code
Interfacethe public functions outside code uses
Class / instanceblueprint / an object made from it

lessons.title: Declaring a class
lessons.html:
A class declaration describes the members of the new type. Here is a class for a bank account:

class Account
{
private:
    double balance;
    double rate;
public:
    void setBalance(double);
    void setRate(double);
    double getBalance() const;
    double getRate() const;
    double getInterest() const;
};     // semicolon required

Rules

  • The key word class, the class name, a body in braces, and a semicolon after the closing brace. Forgetting that semicolon is a classic error.
  • Class names conventionally start with an uppercase letter.
  • An access specifier controls who may use the members that follow it. private: members can be used only by member functions of the class. public: members can be used by any code. With no specifier written, a class treats its members as private. It is good style to write the specifier anyway.
  • A struct is almost the same as a class; the difference is that struct members are public by default.
  • Private and public sections may come in any order and may repeat; grouping them is style, not a rule.
  • Since C++11 a member variable may get a starting value in its declaration, double balance = 0.0; (in-place initialization). Otherwise set it with a constructor or a mutator.

Defining member functions

The class declares a function's prototype. The body can be written outside the class with the scope resolution operator :: after the class name. Without Account:: the compiler would think it is an ordinary function.

void Account::setBalance(double b)
{
    balance = b;
}
double Account::getInterest() const
{
    return balance * rate;
}

Inside a member function you use the member names directly: no dot is needed. A function written entirely inside the class body is also legal (an inline member function).

const member functions

When const appears after the parameter list, the function promises not to change the object's member variables. The compiler rejects an attempt to modify one. const must appear in both the declaration and the definition. Use it for functions that only look at the data.

double Account::getBalance() const   // legal: only reads
{ return balance; }
void Counter::bump() const           // ERROR if it changes a member
{ n++; }

More rules examiners test

  • The class header is just class Name: no colon, no parentheses, and the key word is lowercase class. Each access specifier ends with a colon: private:, public:.
  • Every member function needs a return type (void if it returns nothing). Only constructors and destructors have none.
  • A member function definition header has the form ReturnType ClassName::functionName(parameters) const. The name before :: is the class, the name after it is the function.
  • A const member function may read members but not assign to them: void bump() const { n++; } is an error.
  • A member function can always use the class's private members, const or not. Code outside the class cannot.
  • Before C++11 a constructor had to give member variables their starting values; since C++11 you can write double rate = 0.05; inside the class.

lessons.title: Creating and using objects
lessons.html:
A class declaration creates no objects. You define an object (an instance) the same way you define a variable, with the class name as the type. Defining an object is called instantiation.

Account acct;            // one instance
Account a, b;            // two instances

Each instance has its own copy of the member variables. Changing a does not change b.

The dot operator

To reach a public member of an object from outside the class, write the object name, a dot, and the member: the dot operator.

acct.setBalance(1000);
acct.setRate(0.05);
cout << acct.getInterest();     // 50
acct.balance = 4;               // ERROR: balance is private

A call such as a.getInterest() runs the function on a's data; b.getInterest() runs it on b's data. The object before the dot decides whose member variables are used; inside the member function the members are written by bare name, with no dot. The data an object holds at a given moment is its state. You already use objects this way: name.length() calls a member function of a string object.

Accessors and mutators

An accessor (getter) retrieves a value from an object without changing it; accessors are marked const. A mutator (setter) stores a value in a member variable or otherwise changes it. In the class above, getBalance and getInterest are accessors; setBalance and setRate are mutators.

Assignment and copies

Assigning one object of a class to another copies the member variables one by one. Afterward they are independent copies.

Account p, q;
p.setBalance(300);
q = p;              // q now has balance 300
p.setBalance(900);  // q still 300

Traps

  • Using a class before it is declared, or leaving out the semicolon after the class.
  • Member variables are not automatically set to 0. In an object defined inside a function they hold garbage until something stores a value (a constructor, covered below, solves this).
  • Do not store a value that can be calculated from other members (such as the interest owed): it goes stale when those members change. Calculate it in a member function instead.
  • Calling a non-const function through a const object is an error.

Details used in the examples

  • count += n; means count = count + n;.
  • All objects of a class share the one copy of the member function code, but every object has its own copy of each ordinary member variable.
  • Calling a member function: desk.setWatts(60); (object, dot, function). The :: form belongs in a definition header, not in a call.
  • Inside a member function such as getInterest, the member variable is written as the bare name balance, never acct.balance.
  • An accessor's header ends in const and usually returns a value: double getTarget() const. A function that changes a member, such as void setTarget(double t) or void raise(double amount), is a mutator. A constructor has the class's name and is neither.

lessons.title: Why have private members?
lessons.html:
If member variables were public, any code could assign them directly, including nonsense such as a negative age or a width of zero that later causes a divide-by-zero. The author of the class would have no control over what the data holds.

Making data private

Make the member variables private and provide public member functions as the interface. All outside access then goes through functions the class author wrote. This gives you:

  • Protection: a mutator can check its argument and refuse bad values.
  • Freedom to change the inside: if the class stored an angle in degrees and now stores it in radians, only the member functions change. Code that calls setAngle(90) keeps working.
  • Consistency: related members stay in step. If an object stores both a radius and a diameter, one mutator can update both.
void Person::setAge(int a)
{
    if (a >= 0)
        age = a;      // ignore a bad value
}

With public data this check could not be enforced. The usual design: data private, interface public. Helper functions that only the class itself needs can also be private.

Exam phrasing

"Why should member variables be private?" Best answer: so that they can be accessed or changed only through the class's member functions, which can validate the data and hide how it is stored.

Terms

A mutator (setter) is a public member function that stores or changes a member variable; an accessor (getter) returns a value without changing it. The public member functions together are the class's interface, like a car's pedals and steering wheel, which hide the machinery. Because a mutator can check a value first, private data plus mutators protects the object from bad data, and the storage inside the class can be redesigned without breaking callers.

lessons.title: Constructors and the default constructor
lessons.html:
A constructor is a special member function that runs on its own at the moment an object comes into existence. Its job is to give the object's member variables their starting values.

Rules

  • The constructor's name is identical to the class name.
  • It has no return type, not even void.
  • It is normally public.
  • It runs once for each object created, before anything else is done with the object.
class Box
{
private:
    double width, height;
public:
    Box();                 // default constructor
    Box(double, double);   // takes arguments
    double getArea() const;
};
Box::Box()                 { width = 1; height = 1; }
Box::Box(double w, double h) { width = w; height = h; }

Passing arguments

Put the arguments in parentheses after the object name:

Box a;            // runs Box()        : area 1
Box b(3, 4);      // runs Box(double, double) : area 12

The default constructor

A default constructor is any constructor you can call without supplying arguments: either it has no parameters, or all its parameters have default values. It runs for Box a;.

  • If you write no constructors at all, the compiler supplies a default constructor that does nothing useful to the member variables.
  • If you write any constructor, the compiler no longer supplies one. A class with only Box(double, double) cannot be defined as Box a;: a compile error.
  • Default arguments can combine several versions: Box(double w = 1, double h = 1); works for Box a;, Box a(5); (height 1) and Box a(5, 6);.
  • A class cannot contain two default constructors. If it has both Box() and Box(double w = 1), then Box a; is ambiguous and will not compile.
  • Trap: Box a(); does not create an object. It declares a function. Leave off the parentheses to use the default constructor.

Member initialization list

A constructor can initialize members after a colon, before its body runs: Box::Box() : width(1), height(1) { }. The effect here is the same as assigning in the body.

More constructor facts

  • A class may have several constructors with different parameter lists. The arguments you write in the object definition decide which one runs: Lamp a(40); picks the one-parameter version, Lamp b(40, 20); the two-parameter version.
  • A constructor header may not be const and has no return type: Account(double b); is valid; void Account(double b); and Account(double b) const; are not.
  • Its name must match the class exactly, including capitals. A constructor runs at the moment the object is defined, so output it prints appears between the statements before and after that definition.
  • With default arguments, a missing argument takes its default: given Pt(int a = 0, int b = 0), Pt p(5); sets a to 5 and b to 0.
  • A member initialization list sets members before the body runs; here the body is empty: Timer() : secs(30) { }.
  • A constructor whose parameters all have defaults is also a default constructor. So Lamp() {...} together with Lamp(int w = 60) {...} makes Lamp desk; ambiguous, though Lamp desk(75); is fine.
class Lamp
{
private:
    int watts;
public:
    Lamp(int w) { watts = w; }
    Lamp(int w, int extra) : watts(w + extra) { }
};
Lamp a(40);        // 40 watts
Lamp b(40, 20);    // 60 watts

lessons.title: More class features (first look)
lessons.html:
These topics come up in the same chapter. Know the basic rule for each.

Inline member functions

A member function whose body is written inside the class declaration is an inline member function. It needs no ClassName::. Short accessors are often written this way:

double getBalance() const { return balance; }

Separate files

By convention the class declaration goes in a header file named after the class, Account.h (the specification file), and the member function definitions go in Account.cpp (the implementation file). A program that uses the class writes #include "Account.h", and Account.cpp is compiled and linked with it.

Destructors

A destructor runs automatically when an object is destroyed (for a local object, when its function ends). Its name is a tilde plus the class name, ~Account(). Like a constructor it has no return type; unlike a constructor it takes no arguments, so a class has only one destructor.

Private member functions

A member function declared under private: can be called only by other member functions of the same class. Use it for an internal helper that outside code should never call.

Arrays of objects

Account accts[3]; creates three objects and runs the default constructor for each one. If the class has no default constructor, every element needs an initializer. Call a member function on one element with accts[1].getInterest().

UML class diagrams

A UML class diagram is a box in three parts: the class name, the member variables, the member functions. A - before a member means private and + means public; types are written after a colon, as in - balance : double and + getInterest() : double.

Input and output in a class

Member functions usually return values rather than using cin or cout, so that each program using the class can decide how to get input and show results. That keeps the class reusable.

Reminders

  • An array of objects such as Star sky[4]; runs the default constructor four times, once per element, in order.
  • A destructor for class Lamp is ~Lamp(); a class has at most one, since it takes no arguments.
  • A UML diagram has three boxes: class name, member variables, member functions. - marks private members and + public ones.
  • Small examples may put everything in one file, but the convention is: declaration in Kettle.h (specification file), function definitions in Kettle.cpp (implementation file), and the program #include "Kettle.h".

questions.prompt: Which statement describes procedural programming?
choices: The program is built around objects that contain their own data and functions
The program has no functions, only classes
The program is built around functions, and the data is kept in separate variables passed to them
The data is always hidden from every function
questions.explain: Procedural programming centers on procedures; data and code are separate. Bundling them is the object-oriented approach.

questions.prompt: Combining data and the functions that operate on it into a single object is called ___.
questions.explain: Encapsulation is bundling; data hiding is restricting outside access to the bundled data.

questions.prompt: What is data hiding?
choices: Encrypting the object's data when it is stored on disk
Deleting variables that are no longer used
Giving member variables short, unclear names
Keeping an object's data out of direct reach of code outside the object, so only member functions can use it
questions.explain: Data hiding means outside code goes through member functions. It protects data from accidental corruption.

questions.prompt: Which statement about classes and objects is correct?
choices: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance made from it
A class is an instance of an object
An object is a blueprint; a class is made from it
A class holds the data values; an object only holds functions
questions.explain: One class can produce many objects, each with its own values. The class itself is only the description.

questions.prompt: In OOP terms, the data in an object are its attributes and the procedures it performs are its member functions.
questions.explain: In C++ the attributes are member variables. Other languages call member functions methods.

questions.prompt: A class declaration contains the members below with no access specifier written. What is their access?
choices: public
private
protected, which is visible to all code in the file
None; it is a compile error
questions.explain: When a class declaration names no access specifier, its members are private. A struct is the opposite and defaults to public.

questions.prompt: The access specifier that lets code outside the class use a member is ___.
questions.explain: public members form the interface. private members are reachable only from the class's own member functions.

questions.prompt: What does const after the parameter list of a member function mean?
questions.code: double getArea() const;
choices: The function can only be called once
The function returns a constant value
The function may not modify the object's member variables
The member variables become public
questions.explain: const member functions only read data. The compiler gives an error if they assign to a member.

questions.prompt: The compiler accepts the class declaration below, which is followed directly by `main`.
questions.explain: A class declaration must end with a semicolon after its closing brace. Without it the compiler reports an error, usually pointing at the next line.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct header for defining the const member function getInterest of class Account outside the class?
choices: double getInterest() const
double Account.getInterest() const
double Account:getInterest() const
double Account::getInterest() const
questions.explain: Use the class name and the scope resolution operator ::. A dot is for objects, and a single colon is not an operator here.

questions.prompt: When a member function is defined outside its class, the class name is followed by the ___ operator (written ::).
questions.explain: The scope resolution operator ties the definition to the class so the compiler knows which class's function it is.

questions.prompt: Why does this class fail to compile?
choices: bump is const but modifies the member variable n
n is private so bump cannot use it
A class may not have a function named bump
The class is missing a return type for bump
questions.explain: Member functions can always use private members. A const member function, though, may not change them.

questions.prompt: The operator used to access a member of an object, as in box.getArea(), is the ___ operator.
questions.explain: The dot operator joins an object name and one of its public members.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: setCount stores 5, then two add calls make 5 + 3 + 4 = 12.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: Each Box object has its own width and height. a is 2 by 3 and b is 4 by 5.

questions.prompt: A member function that stores a value in a member variable is called a(n) ___.
choices: accessor
mutator
constructor
stub
questions.explain: Mutators (setters) change data. Accessors (getters) only return it.

questions.prompt: The class Account has a private member balance and public functions deposit, getBalance and setOwner. Which statement in main causes a compile error?
choices: acct.deposit(50);
cout << acct.getBalance();
acct.balance = 100;
acct.setOwner("Lee");
questions.explain: balance is private, so code outside the class cannot use it with the dot operator. The public member functions are fine.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: q = p copies the members. After that p and q are separate objects, so adding 3 to p does not change q.

questions.prompt: Two objects of the same class share a single copy of the member variables.
questions.explain: Each object has its own copy of every ordinary (non-static) member variable. Only the member function code is shared.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of making member variables private and providing public mutators?
choices: The program runs faster
The variables use less memory
No member functions are needed
Mutators can check values before storing them, and the inside of the class can change without breaking other code
questions.explain: Private data forces all changes through functions that can validate, and hides the data layout. It does not affect speed or memory.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: setAge ignores a negative argument, so the age stays 20 after the second call. With a public variable this protection would not exist.

questions.prompt: If a class keeps its data private, its internal storage can be redesigned without changing the code that calls its public member functions.
questions.explain: The public functions are the interface. As long as they behave the same, callers do not care how the data is stored.

questions.prompt: The public member functions through which outside code works with an object are called its ___.
questions.explain: A simple interface hides the complicated internals, like the pedals and steering wheel of a car.

questions.prompt: A member function that is called automatically when an object is created is a ___.
questions.explain: The constructor initializes the object. It runs once per object, when the object is defined.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid declaration of a constructor taking one double for the class Account?
choices: Account(double b);
void Account(double b);
account(double b);
Account(double b) const;
questions.explain: A constructor has the class's exact name and no return type, not even void. Constructors are not const.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: Box a uses the default constructor (1 by 1, area 1). Box b(3, 4) uses the two-argument constructor.

questions.prompt: What is a default constructor?
choices: The constructor that runs when the program ends
A constructor that can be called with no arguments
A constructor that has a void return type
The only constructor a class is allowed to have
questions.explain: A default constructor has no parameters (or all parameters have defaults) and runs for a definition like Box a;.

questions.prompt: Why does this code fail to compile?
choices: Constructors cannot have parameters
Rect r; needs parentheses: Rect r();
The class has a constructor with parameters, so the compiler supplies no default constructor for Rect r;
The constructor must return a value
questions.explain: Writing any constructor cancels the automatic default one. Add Rect() or give the parameters default values. Rect r(); would declare a function.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: The default arguments fill in missing values: Pt a uses 0 and 0, Pt b(5) uses y = 0, and Pt c(5, 6) uses both arguments.

questions.prompt: A constructor is declared with the return type void.
questions.explain: A constructor has no return type at all, not even void.

questions.prompt: Defining an object of a class, as in `Account acct;`, is called the ___ of the class.
questions.explain: The object created is an instance of the class. A class declaration alone instantiates nothing.

questions.prompt: If no access specifier is written, members of a struct are public, while members of a class are private.
questions.explain: That default is the main difference between the two. Otherwise classes and structs are very similar in C++.

questions.prompt: Look at this member function header. What is the function's name, and which class is it a member of?
questions.code: void Lamp::setWatts(int w)
choices: Name Lamp, member of class setWatts
Name void, member of class Lamp
Name Lamp::setWatts, not a member of any class
Name setWatts, member of class Lamp
questions.explain: In ReturnType ClassName::functionName(parameters), the name before :: is the class and the name after it is the function. void is the return type.

questions.prompt: Class Lamp has a public void member function setWatts that takes an int. desk is a Lamp object. Which statement correctly calls setWatts for desk?
choices: desk.setWatts(60);
desk::setWatts(60);
Lamp::setWatts(60);
setWatts(desk, 60);
questions.explain: Call a member function with the object, the dot operator and the function name. :: belongs in the header of a member function definition, not in a call.

questions.prompt: In a class declaration, all private members must be declared before the public members.
questions.explain: public and private sections may come in any order and may even appear more than once. Grouping each kind together is good style, not a rule.

questions.prompt: Class Thermostat has these member functions. Which one is an accessor?
choices: void setTarget(double t)
double getTarget() const
void raise(double amount)
Thermostat()
questions.explain: An accessor returns a member's value without changing it, so it is marked const. setTarget and raise change data (mutators), and Thermostat() is a constructor.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: A constructor runs automatically at the moment the object is defined. g is defined between the two cout statements, so its message appears between them.

questions.prompt: Class Account has private double members balance and rate and no constructor. Inside main, `Account acct;` is defined. What do balance and rate hold right after this statement?
choices: 0 and 0, because member variables start at zero
1 and 1
Nothing, because the statement is a compile error
Unpredictable garbage values, until something stores values in them
questions.explain: Member variables are not automatically set to 0. Using them before storing a value gives garbage, which is why a constructor that sets them is a good idea.

questions.prompt: Account stores balance and rate but has no interest member; getInterest() calculates balance * rate each time it is called. Why is that the better design?
choices: Multiplication is not allowed inside a member variable declaration
A stored interest figure would go stale: it would be wrong as soon as balance or rate changed
A class may not have more than two member variables
getInterest would have to be private if the interest were stored
questions.explain: Data that depends on other data becomes stale when the other data changes and it does not. Calculating the value on request always gives the current answer.

questions.prompt: Inside the definition of Account::getInterest, how does the code refer to the calling object's balance member?
choices: acct.balance
Account.balance
balance
getInterest.balance
questions.explain: A member function has direct access to the members of the object that called it, so it uses the bare name. For acct.getInterest() that is acct's balance; for another object's call it is that object's balance.

questions.prompt: string is a class, and word is an object of it. What does this code print? Assume the code is inside main(), with iostream and string included and using namespace std; in effect.
questions.explain: append and length are member functions called through the object with the dot operator. append adds "house" to the stored text, and length returns its 9 characters.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: The part after the colon is a member initialization list: secs(30) sets secs before the empty body runs. Timer a uses the default constructor and Timer b(90) the one that takes an int.

questions.prompt: Why does `Lamp desk;` fail to compile with this class?
choices: A constructor cannot have a default argument
Both constructors can be called with no arguments, so the call is ambiguous; a class cannot have two default constructors
Lamp desk; needs empty parentheses: Lamp desk();
watts must be public for a constructor to set it
questions.explain: A constructor whose parameters all have defaults is also a default constructor, so the compiler cannot choose. Lamp desk(75); would compile, because only the second constructor takes one argument.

questions.prompt: Since C++11, a member variable may be given an initial value in its declaration inside the class, as in `double rate = 0.05;`.
questions.explain: This is in-place initialization. Before C++11 a constructor (or its member initialization list) had to set starting values.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a destructor is true?
choices: It is named with a tilde and the class name, has no return type and no parameters, and runs automatically when the object is destroyed
It can take any number of arguments, like a constructor
It must be called explicitly at the end of main
It returns true when the object was destroyed successfully
questions.explain: For class Lamp the destructor is ~Lamp(). It cannot return a value or take arguments, so a class has only one destructor.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: Defining an array of objects runs the default constructor once for each element, not only for the first one.

questions.prompt: A member function whose body is written inside the class declaration is called an ___ member function.
questions.explain: Short functions such as accessors are often written this way. A body written outside the class needs ClassName:: in its header.

questions.prompt: By the usual convention, where are the declaration of class Kettle and the definitions of its member functions stored?
choices: Both in the file that contains main
The declaration in Kettle.cpp and the member function definitions in Kettle.h
The declaration in Kettle.h (the specification file) and the member function definitions in Kettle.cpp (the implementation file)
The declaration in Kettle.exe and the definitions in Kettle.obj
questions.explain: A program that uses the class includes Kettle.h, and Kettle.cpp is compiled and linked with it. Small examples may keep everything in one file, but this split is the convention.

questions.prompt: In a UML class diagram, what does a minus sign (-) in front of a member name mean?
choices: The member is private
The member is public
The member is a constructor
The member returns a negative value
questions.explain: UML marks private members with - and public members with +. The diagram's three parts hold the class name, the member variables and the member functions.

questions.prompt: Code in main can call a private member function of a class, as long as it uses an object and the dot operator.
questions.explain: A private member function can be called only by other member functions of the same class. Make a function private when it is an internal helper that outside code should not call.

questions.prompt: Which list names every error in this class declaration?
choices: Only the missing semicolon after the closing brace
The colon after Lamp, the missing colons after private and public, no return type on setWatts, and no semicolon after the closing brace
watts must be public, and the key word must be written Class
The colon after Lamp and the missing semicolon; everything else is legal
questions.explain: The header is just class Lamp, each access specifier ends in a colon, every member function other than a constructor or destructor needs a return type (void here), and the declaration ends with };.

questions.prompt: This code fails to compile. What is wrong?
choices: kg must be public for setKg to use it
setKg cannot take a parameter
A class may not have a member named kg
The definition header lacks Scale::, so it defines an ordinary function that cannot see kg
questions.explain: Without Scale:: the function is not the member, so the name kg means nothing inside it. The header should be void Scale::setKg(int k).

questions.prompt: Why do class designers usually avoid putting cin and cout statements inside member functions such as setWidth or getArea?
choices: cin and cout cannot be used inside a class
Member functions run before main, when the screen is not ready
The class would be tied to one way of doing input and output, making it harder to reuse; the program using the class should handle the I/O
It would make the member variables public
questions.explain: A class that prompts or prints on its own forces that behavior on every program that uses it. Returning values and letting the calling program display them keeps the class reusable.

questions.prompt: What is an object's state?
choices: The data stored in its member variables at a given moment
The list of member functions its class declares
Whether its class is public or private
The file in which its class is declared
questions.explain: Calling mutators changes an object's state. Two objects of the same class usually have different states.

programs.title: Account class with constructors
programs.task:
Write a class named Account with a private double member balance.
- A default constructor sets the balance to 0.
- A constructor taking one double sets the starting balance.
- deposit(double amount) adds the amount only if it is greater than 0.
- withdraw(double amount) returns bool: it subtracts the amount and returns true only if the amount is greater than 0 and not more than the balance; otherwise it changes nothing and returns false.
- getBalance() const returns the balance.
In main: create Account a(100) and Account b (default). Read three numbers from the user: a deposit, then two withdrawals. Deposit into a, then attempt the first withdrawal; if it fails display "Withdrawal of X refused" (X is the amount). Then make the second withdrawal. Display "Balance: " and a's balance, then "Empty account: " and b's balance, one per line.
